36G THE TRIUMPHS OF THE GOSPEL IN THE CORAL ISLANDS.

conversion. The outward habits were changed; the ohdurnte heart remained unaffected. The truths of Christianity were received as truths, hnt not as_ truths to affect the heart. The social condition of the people had been improved; their huts were more substantially built; their laws against crime were more righteous; their magi8tracy and police force were less rudely organised; and the arts of civilisation were introduced. U nfortnnately, however, Christianity for a time suffered through the sad defection of one of the native teachers. The heathen priests thereupon ,owed that the new religion should he destroyed, or they would die. The chapel and the houses of the Christians were fired; the missionaries 'l>ere reduced to poverty, were laid low by disease, and almost swept into the jaws of death by a fi0od. The natives were attacked by the epidemic, from which one hundred a day died. However, the work of God prospered. Children were educated; the Sabbath-day was kept; classes for the instruction of the natives were formed; and but for a fearful hurricane 'l>hich visited the island, all would have gone on pleasantly. Yet this did not materially hinder the spread of Christian truth. The mission-houses that had been destroyed were rebuilt, a printing-press was introduced; and the natives themselves who had received the truth into their hearts, went forth to the islands of the Samoan group to tell to others the way to happiness and life eternal. It was not until six years had elapsed that it was thought advisable to form a Christian church in Rarotonga. But the work had been tested sufficiently, and so in May, 1833, the converts were organised into a religicus community. Marriage ties were not only respected, but polygamy was dying out in the stations where Christianity flourished. Another missionary was needed to alternately visit the islands of the group, and to extend and consolidate the mterest of the whole, and the London Missionary Society, which had sent out the first two European Missionaries, appointed Mr. W. Gill, who sailed in the year 1838. A marvellously cheap and beautifully got up edition of Mr. Gill's record of sixteen years' labour in Lhese islands, has just been published,* and the book deserves to be placed side by side with Williams' and Moffatt's well-known works of Christian adventure. When Mr. Gill landed he was delighted with the prospect that was before him. " It was," be says, "a wonderful and overpowering sight, my first Sabb~th on shore to see this house of prayer filled with more than 1,600 native worshippers with but few exceptions, clothed in white native cloth ; and to rem;mber that only ten years before this, they were wild naked heathens, but now subdued, and a goodly number of them thir;;ting for instruction which should still further dignify and bless them." Five thousand copies of the New Testament, printed in their own language, were sold to the natives. In 18-!3, the population of Rarotonga was three thousand three hundred, and the total number in communion was 408, while 850 were in ad u It schools and 1 300 in children's schools. Another chapel was erected by the ~atives 'who took great interest in the work. Nothing could be more remark~ble than the change of life which came over the ~ Gems from the Coral lsl,i,nds, or Incidents of Contrast between Savage and Christian Life. Yates and Alexander, Cllancery Lane.

converts. Their simplicity was singular, and their zeal great. One of the deacons had been a cannibal, and was known as" always having human flesh on his meat-hol)k." When he came to die, he was much troubled because of his sins and murders, but reminded that "the blood of Jesus Christ cleanseth from all sin," he exclaimed "Yes, he is my Justifier, and my Priest, and no sinner has ever been cast away by him." An institution was formed for the education of a native ministry, who should serve as pioneers in the mission field-a plan of the utmost importance. Four converts were sent out as evangelists to the heathen ; up to 1852 one hundred students had been admitted. A terrible hurricane tried the work, for the ruin was exceeding great ; but in less than five years, on this and another island there were built twelve large and substantial chapels and school-houses, three mission-houses and three hundred stone cottages; all testifying to the Christian earnestness of the people and the power both of the gospel and of civilisation over their Ii ves. Subsequently a spirit of revival was felt among the churches, and as a result five hundred enquirers manifested concern for salvation, three hundred of whom were known to remain consistent Christians. If liberality to the cause of Christ be an index of piety, then the native converts not only of this but of the other islands of the group, must be commended for their religious zeal and practical godliness. Small as is the population of the islands, and poor as are the majority of the people, yet they have manifested a liberality that might put many English Christians to the blush. The island of Mare has a population of about six thonsand persons, who, before the light of the gospel had dawned on their land, were equally as barbarous as the natives of Rarotonga. They worshipped an unseen power, through the medium of stones and wood; and the way in which they preserved and held as sacred the relics of priests and heroes testified to their degradation. The eyelashes and hair were preserved; the finger-nails and toe-nails extracted, and were consecrated, and kept with care as mediums of communication between the people and their gods. "In drought," relates Mr. Gill, " two sacred men, having, as an act of humiliation, besmeared their bodies from head to foot with a mixture of lampblack and mud, visited the grave of some renowned person ; every bone of the corpse was then carefully cleansed, and with the skill of practised anatomists, the priests carefully re-united bone to bone, until the skeleton was complete. This work was performed in a consecrated cave; and hanging up the skeleton, water was poured upon it by the men, who at the same t\~e presen_ted prayer to the gods for rain. It was supposed that the spmt of then· departed heroes had power with the gods to convey this oblation of water into the heavens, and who, by being thus propitiated, would create clouds, and again cause rain to fall on their famishing land." We are also informed, that the priests never left the place until the rain came, and the rain failing, have even been known to die there. The inhabitants were cannibals, and their warlike habits were abominable. Fathers would eat sons, and sons eat fathers, and the moral condition of the islanders was so low that the men were regarded as wild beasts of a most ferocious type. Englishmen who had visited the island had been massacred, and their

bodies eaten. So great was their hatred of white people, that it is probable th~y would never have received the truths of the gospel from them; and it was fortunate that educated, intelligent natives from Rarotonga were the first to endeavour to impress their minds in favour of true religion. In two years, they had insinuated themselves into the rude affections of the people; had taught them some of the arts of ci,ilisation, and had gathered around them a class of heathen youth~. In a time of sickness, these youths saved their teachers from beino· killed and en,ten as a sacrifice to the gods, and in u. time of perseculio~ they also saved their lives from their enemies. Amid many trials and difficulties, the mission advanced, conquering the prejudices of the heathen, overcoming their vicious and barbarous habits, and bringinglight and joy where darkness and sin had reigned. A chapel was erected, converts avowed themselves to be on the side of Christ, EngJi5h missionaries undertook the work ; and now seven villages are under Christian instruction, while native teachers, Sunday-school teachers, and native missionaries, with a large number of church members, :md enquirers, and scholars, tell of the wonderful change which God has wrought in this island. The same story, full of unique details, is related of the other islands of the group that have been evangelised by native teachers mainly. Nothing can exceed in interest the story of the conversion to Christ of the wild inhabitants of these islands. They did not relinquish their idolatrous practices without a severe struggle. In some cases, treating the Christian missionaries as enemies, they were anxious to fight, them. But perseverance was rewarded with abundant success. Heathenism and idolatry were renounced, and the truth of the gospel acknowledged. That they had but imperfect notions of their duty is to be expected; but in their simplicity the_y were most desirous of being taught. '' I~ it a sin to eat raw fish ?" "T s it wrong to eat half-cooked pork?" "Does the Bible allow wives to sit at meals with their husbands ?" ;, Is it ri(Tht 0 to be angr_y at the birth of girls instead of boys?" "Is it wronCT to eat rats?" These and many other similar questions affecting old diet, aod habits, and lives, agitated their minds and needed solution lw the missionary. Naturally of simple minds, they were open to instruction, and convinced of the rightfulness of relinquishing old customs, they gladly overcame them. Many of the old people declined to give up their own superstition; it had been the. religion ?f their fathers and it was good enough for them, though their sons might do as they pleased. The education of the youths was therefore the great hope of the missionaries, aud happily, through the divine blessing, this has been accomplished. In one case, the fertile island of Aitutaki, the inhabitants of which were the first heathen that Mr. Williams had ever seen, no opposition was shown to the introduction of Christianity. Iodeed, the idols were soon burnt, the profession of the gospel became creneral and not a single idolato1· remained on the island ; and these ;ere re~ults due, under God, to the teaching of native evangelist~. Of course, all who professed Christianity were not Christians. Cases of defection have been known ; missionaries were not always well treated; the evil influences of heathen superstitions and immorality and barb:irou:s customs were not wholly banished. But, as in England, so in the

but "the glorious gospel of the blessed God" could work so great a miracle as may be seen in the Coral Islands? Civilisation has done much to elevate man's moral and social character; though even the civilised have done more to degrade their fellow beings than their moral principles have benefited them. Englishmen have visited these islands and have sought to make the natives greater lovers of vice than ever. They did all that was in the power of civilised sinners to ruin the future prospects of the gospel; and the first obstacle against which the missionaries had to contend was the conduct of their own countrymen in the islands. But the simple lessons of a Redeemer's love have changed the moral, social, and religious aspects of the islands; and from one island to another native teachers and English missionaries have journeyed, labouring in the strength of the Lord. The facts recorded in Mr. Gill's most interesting volume are encouraging, and should be incentives to farther action. "There are still," he says, "upwards of two hundred islands, in the North and South Pacific Oceans, where the inhabitants are in the same state of idolatry and degradation as the South Sea Islanders once were." Since these islands are for the most part accessible, it is to be hoped that they may be soon visited by native converts and missionaries, so that other chapters may be added to the records of J ehovah's triumphs.

THEduction :Rev. J. G. Woods relates a curious Jewish legend respecting the introof the starling into Palestine :- " Many years ago a strange bird appeared in Jerusalem. It was cauo-ht and brought before a celebrated Rabbi for examination, in order that"'h; might._ decide whether it belonged to the clean or the unclean birds. After examining it, he could not make up his mind to either side of the question, and left the disputed point to be settled in a different wt1,y. He ordered the bird to be pbced on the roof of a house, and to be carefully watched, in order that the birds which associ~ted with it might b~ noticed. For some time no birds of any kiud would reco()'n1se the str,in~er, until at fast there came a raven from E"ypt which claimed a[quaintance witn it. to what you liave to do all the day m the ordmary business of it. We are weak and forgetful, and need to be put in mincl of our duty in "eneral, upon e,·ery occasion for the doing of it ; and therefore I choose to be tl~us particnla.r, that I may be your remembrancer. • lrlwn yoii meet with your .familus in the morning wait upon God for a blessing upon them, and attend him with your thankscrivincrs for the mercies you and yonrs have jointly received from God the nigl1t p~st ; you and your houses must serve the Lord, must wait on him. It is owing to his goodness who is the founder and Father of the families of the righteous, that you are together, that the voice of rejoicing and salvation is in your tabernacles, and therefore wait upon him to continue you together, to make you comforts to one another, to enable you to do the duty of every relation, and to lengthen out the days of your tranquility. In all the conversation we have with our families, the provision we make for them, and the orders we give concerning them, we must wait upon God, as ' the God of all the families of Israel' (J er. xxxi. 1) ; and have an eye to Christ as he ' in whom all the families of the earth are blessed.' Every member of the family sharing in family mercies, must wait on God for grace to contribute to family duties. Whatever disagrl!eableness there may be in any family-relation, instead of having the spirit either bUidened with it, or provoked by it, let it be an inducement to wait on God, who is able either to .edress the grievance, or to balance it, and give grace to bear it. ITTien you are pu!_suj_11g the education of your children, or the young ones under yoDI charge, wait upon God for his grace to make the means of their education successful. ,vhen you are yourselves giving them instruction in things pertaining either to life or godliness, their general or particular calling, when you are sending them to school in a morning, or ordering them the business of the day, wait upon God to give them an understanding, and a good capacity for their business, especially their main business, 'for it is God that giveth wisdom.' If tbey are but slow, and do not come on as you could wish, yet wait on God to bring them forward, and to give them his grace in his own time ; and 'll"hile you are patiently waiting on him, that will encourage you to take pains with them, and will likewise make you patient and gentle towards them. And let children and young people wait on God in all their daily endeavours to fit themselves for tbe service of God and their generation. Yon desire to be comforts to yoDI relations--to be good for something in this world-do you not 1 Beg of God then a wise and an understanding heart, as Solomon did, and wait upon him all the day for it, that you may still be increasing in wisdom, as you do in stature, and in favour with God and man. When you go to your shops, or apply yourselves to the business of ;rour particular calling, wait upon God for his presence with you. Your busmess calls for your constant attendance, every day, and all the day ; keep thy shop, :.md thy shop will keep thee • but let your attendance on God in your callings be as constant as your attenda~ce on your callings. Eye God's provi~ence in all the occurrences of them. Open shop with this thought, "I am now m the _,~ay of my duty, and I depend upon God to bless me in it." When yo~ are wa1t(ng fur customers, wait on God to find you something to do in that calling to which he bath called you; those you call chance-customers, you should rather call pro,idence-customers, and should say of the advantage Y_OU make b;r them, "The Lord my God brought it to me." When you are buymg and sellmg, see God's eye upon you to observe whether you are honest and just in your dealings, and do no wrong to those you deal with ; and let your eye then be up to him for that discretion to which God doth instruct not only the husbandman but the

expected in the way of honest diligence. Whatever your employments bein country-business, city-business, or sea-business-or only in the business of the house, go about them in the fear of God, depending upon him to make them comforta.ble and successful, iind to prosper the work of your hands unto you. And hereby you will arm yourselves against many temptations you are compassed about with in your worldly business: by waiting on God, you will be freed from that care and cumber which attends much serving, will have your minds raised above the little things of sense and time, will be serving God then when you me most busy about the world, and will have God in your hearts, when your hands are full of the world. When you take a book into your hand-~, God's book, or any other usefol goocl book, wait upon God for his grace to enable you to make a good use of it. Some of you spend a deal of time every ddy in reading, and I hope none of yGtl let a day pass without reading some portions of Scripture, either alone or wi,h. your families. Take heed that the time you spend in reading be not lost time; it is so if you read that which is idle, and vain, and unprofitable ; it is so if you read that which is good, even the word of God itself, and do not mind it, or observe it, or aim to m,ike it of any advantage to yon; wait upon God, who gives you those helps for your souls, to make them helpful indeed to you. The eunuch did so when he was reading the book of the prophet Isaiah in his chariot, and God presently sent him one who made him understand what he read. You read perhaps now and then the histories of former times; in acquainting yourselves with them, you must have an eye to God, and to that wise and gracious providence which governed the world before we were born, and preserl'ed the church in it, and therefore may still be depended upon to do all for the best, for he is Israel's king of old. When you sit down to your tables, wait on God, see his hand spreading and preparing a table before you in despite of your enemies, and in the society of your friends. Often review the grant which God made to our first father Adam, and in him to us, of the products of the earth. Gen. i. 29. 'Behold, I htwe given you every herb beariug seed,' bread-corn, especially " to you it shall be for meat;" and the grant he afterwards made to Noal1 our seconcl. father, and in him to us. Gen. ix. 3. "Every moving thing th,tt li velh shall be meat for you, even as the greeu herb ; " and see in those wlmt ::i, bountiful benefactor he is to mankind, aud wait upon him accordingly. \Ve must eat ::i,nd drink to the glory of God, and then we wait on him in euting und drinking. "\Ve must receive nourishment for our bodies, that they may be fitted to serve our souls in the service of God, to his honour in this world. "\Ve must taste covenant-love in common mercies, and enjoy the Creator while we are using the creature. "\Ve must depend upon the word of blessing from the mouth of God, to m,ike our food nourishing to us; and if our provisions be mean aud scanty, we must make up the want of them by faith in the promise of God, and rejoice in him as the God of our salvation, though the fig-tree doth not blossom, and there is no fruit in the vine. JV!ten you visit your friends, or receive their visits, wait upou Goel; let your eye be to him with thankfulness for your friends and acquaintance, that y,iu h,we comfort in-that the wilderness is not made your h,ibit,1tion, and th~ solitary desert land your dwelling-that you h,we comfort not only in your own housos, but in those of your neighbours, with whom you have freedom of converse-and tlrnt you are not driven out from among men, ,iud m,1de ,i burden and terror to all ,ibout you. That you have clothing not only for nece,- sity but for ornament to go abroad in, is a mercy which, that we may 1:ot pride ourselves in, we must t,1ke notice of God in ; ' I decked thee ,ilsu wtth orn,iment~,• saith God, 'and put ear-rings in thine ea.rs.' Ezek. xvi. 11, 1:l. T~.it you havo houses, furniture, nud entertair,ment, not only for yourseln', but :c,r ;·otll"

good, and_ to the use of edifying, and which may minister grace to the hearers, that our hps may feed many. IT?1c11 you gil'r alms, or do any act of chai·ity, wait on God-do it as unto him-give to a disciple in the name of a disciple, to the poor because they bel_ong to Christ ; do it not for the praise of men, but for the glory of God, with a smgle eye and an upright heart; direct it to him, and then your alms as well as your prayers, like those of Cornelius, come up for a memorial before God. Acts x. -1. Beg of God to accept what you do for the good of others, that your alms may indeed be offerings (Acts xxiv. 17)-may be 'an odour of a sweet smell_, a sacrifice acceptable, well pleasing to God.' Phil. iv. 18. Desire of God a blessmg npon what yon give in charity, that it may be comfortable to those to w~10m it is given ; and that though what you are able to give is but a little, like the widow's two mites, yet that by God's blessing it may be doubled, and made to go a great way, like the widow's meal in the barrel and oil in the cruse. Depend upon God tlo make up t.o you what you lay out in good works, and to recompense it abundantiy in the resurrection of the just; nay, and you are encouraged to wait upon h m for a return of it even in this life. It is bread cast upon the waters which you shall find again after many days ; and you should carefully obserre the prondence of God, whether it do not make you rich amends for your good works, according to the promise, that you may understand the lovingkindness of the Lord, and bis faithfulness to the word which be hath spoken. W7ien you enquire after public news, in that wait upon God ; do it with an eye to him ; for this reason, because you are truly concerned for the interests of his kingdom in the world; and lay them near your hearts because you have 11, compassion for mankind, for the lives and souls of men, and especially of God's people. .A.sk what news? not as the Athenians, only to satisfy a vain curiosity, an!l to pass away an idle hour or two, but that you may know how to direct your prayers and praises, and how to balance your hopes and fe11,rs, and may gain such an understanding of the times, as to learn w);tat you and others ought to do. If the face of public affairs be bright and pleasing, wait upon God to carry on and perfect his own work ; and depend not upon the wisdom or strength of any instruments ; if it be dark and discouraging, wait upon God t~ prevent t~e fears of his people, and to appear for them when he sees that their stre~gth is gone. In the midst of the greatest successes of the church, and t~e smile~ of second causes, we must not think it needless to wait on God ; and m the m~dst of its greatest discouragements, when its affairs are reduced to the last extremity, we must not thiDk it fruitless to wait upon God ; for creatures cannot help without him, but he can help without them. . When you are going journeys, wait on God, put yourself under his protection, commit yourselves to his care, and depend upon him to give his angels_ a char~e concerning you, to bear you up in their arms when you move, and to pitch their tents ;,bout you where you rest. See how much you are indebted to the goodness of his providence for all the comforts and conveniences you are surrounded with ill your travels. It is he that has cast our lot in a land -where we wander not in wildernesses, as in the deserts of Arabia, but have safe and b~aten roads ; and that through the terrors of war the highways are not unoccupied ; to him we owe it that the inferior creatures are serviceable to us, and that onr goings out and comings in are preserved ; that when we are abroad we are not in banishment, but have liberty to come home again; and.when we are at home, we are not under confinement, but have liberty to go abroad. W~ must therefore have our eyes up to God at our setting out, "Lo~d, g? alo_ng with me where I go ; " under his shelter we must travel, confidwg Ill his _care of u_s, and encouraging ourseh·es with that in all the dangers we meet with ; and 111 our

we with him. We shall find temptations even in solitude, which we have need ,to guard against. Satan set upon our Saviour when he was alone in the wilderness. But there also we have opportunity-if we know but how to improve it -for that devout, that divine contemplation, which is the best conversation, so that we may never be less alone than when alone. If when we sit alone and keep silence, withdrawn from business and conversation, we have but the art, I should say the heart, to fill up those vacant minutes with pious meditations of God and divine things, we then gather up the fragments of time which remain, that nothing may be lost, and so are we found waiting on God all the day.

"AL THOUGH_ in the visible church the evil be ever mingled with the good, and sometimes the evil have chief authority in the ministration of the Word and Sacraments, yet forasmuch as they do not the same in their own name, but in Christ's, and do minister by h.is commission and authority, we may use their ministry, both in hearing the Word of God, and in receiving of the sacraments. Neither is the effect of Christ's ordinance taken away by their wickedness, nor the grace of God's gifts diminished from such as by faith and rightly do receive the sacraments ministered unto them: which be effectual, because of Christ's institution and promise, although they be administered by evil men. Nevertheless, it appertaineth to the discipline of the church that enquiry be made of evil ministers, and that they be accused by those that have knowledge of their offences ; and finally being found guilty, by just judgment be deposed." Here are two propositions which, if they were now put forth for the first time by any but Papists and Ritualists, would excite astonishment and grief amongst all true Christians. Only imagine certain evangelical bishops, deans, and rectors, that we could name, publishing in a locale of their own these statements of this Article, what an outcry there would be of " Sacramentalism," " Popery," etc., "among the prophets ;" and how would godly churchmen exclaim, "Wh,,t next/" But the article is three hundred years old, and has been subscribed by a hundred thousand good, bad, and indifferent clergymen of every school, and " what everybody says must be true;" that is, a corporate conscience cannot be wrong, especi,,lly when it is the corporate consciences of good men. Need I remark that such a conscience God does not recognise 1 \Ve shall be judged, not as communities, but as individuals, and, therefore, "we should count money after our fathers," lest a paternal mistake should ruin us. Let us, then, look at the said article from the standpoint of to-day, and ex,,mine it as freely as if it h,,d just issued from the Convoc,,tion of 1869. . Fil'st.-It is affirmed, ex cathedrci, "tlmt sometimes evil men hitve cluq authority in the ministmtiou of the ,v ord and Sacrnments, and that they minister by Christ's _commission and authority."

to all appearance are good and true. But is this shocking statement scriptural 1 Nay, is it not blasphemous? What! an adulterer, impenitent, a.nd still breaking the seventh commandment· yea, a murderer, preaching, baptising, and administering the bread and wine; "b_y the commission :rnd authority of Christ!" According to the canons, the holiest saint in the world, who finds fault with the Prayer Book is excommunicated " ipso facto," without judge or jury-but according to this article the filthiest sinner on earth, who is in "holy orders" though his filthiness be notorious, may continue his ministry, "by the com:nissidn and authority of Christ," until he be found guilty in open court, and "be deposed." What is this but to make Christ himself responsible for the scandal of such ministers'? and what is this but blasphemy 1 Secondly.-As a corollary to this proposition, it is declared tbat Christians "may use the ministry" of these "evil men'' both in hearing the Word of God and in receiving the sacrament," of course, if they preach, and administer the ordinances "by the authority of Christ." But what a reductio ad naiuearn ! A child of God '' may" (according to the canons be must) listen to the known hypocritical preaching of a child of the devil, in '' holy orders," and receive the Lord's Supper from his visibly filthy hands. This too is fathered on Christ! who "promises'' the " gr-.tce of God's gifts'' to all believers, through " the ministrations of evil men." If all this is not the very quintessence of Papery, which makes office and rite everything, officer and admiuistrator nothing, then the question, "what is in a name?" has no force, and Popery called Protestantism loses name and character together. Nay, if all this is not blasphemy, then" Christ and Belia!'' have "fellowship" in the most sacred offices of religion. Baptismal regeneration and episcopal confirmation are bad, very bad; but the doctrines of this Twenty-sixth Article are incomparably worse. After this, I need not add one word about evangelical clerical subscription, or evangelical lay sanction. I'subscribe myself,

THE re-issue of this book, by William Cobbett, is quite a sign of the times : it shows the serious questioning which exercises the public mind as to establishments in general, and the English church in particular. In all Cobbett's political sentiments no man can uniformly agree, for he demolishes to-day what he built up yesterday, and only a chameleon mind could keep pace with him ; but his style is gigantic, Titanic, tremendous ; his language is so simple and Saxon, that no one is ever troubled to know what he means, and yet so forcible that one feels as if each sentence would knock you down. He smites like a huge steam hammer. The clergy, in his hands, are kneaded like dough. 'l'he State church is like an egg-shell on an anvil. He is conscious of such an excess of strength that he plays with his victims as a cat with a mouse. What he was himself in religion we do not know: we should imagine that religious enthusiasm never gained admission into his cool, self-reliant mind. He is nothing as a teacher or repairer of breache,, but he is a splendid battering-ram, and thathappens to be an instrm~ent ii:i large request just now. His designs were very remote from ours, and his notions of the benefits bestowed by the old monastic system we smile at ; but as to the Anglican e,tablishment, the man is very near the truth, and his hard-hitting is richly deserved. His Legacy to Par.vons consists of six letters, dedicated to James Bloru!ield, Bishop of Loudon, who is very cooly told- " It is now become a question seriously, publicly and practically entertained, whether you and your brethren of the established churcl1 should be legally deprived of [l,11 your enormous tomporal possessions; and also whether your whole order should not, as a thing supported by the law, be put an end to for ever. These questions must now be discussed. '£hey are not to be shuffled off by commissions u '.enquiry, or any other commissions; the people demand a discussion of these questions, and a decision upon them; the Parliament must discuss them; and this little book, which I now dedicate to you, is written for the purpose of aiding us all in the discussion, so that we mn.y come at last to " just decision." The first letter answers the question, how came there to be an established church 1 The importance of the question is stated very plainly :- " PARSONs,-This question ought to be cleitrly answered, because on it must turn the great pr:i.ctica.l question no'!" at issue, namely, has the Parliament the rightful p01.cer .'o a.<sume to taJce possession of, and to dispose of, the tithes and all other property, commonly called church p,·operty, in wliatever manner it may thinh proper? You anc'. your p;1rtis;1ns contend that it has not this rightful powe,; I contend that it has." Cobbett, after stating the tenure upon which the church of Rome pretended to hold its position, demands very peremptorily: - " But, parsons, has your church any such pt·etensions? I have a high opinion of that quality in you which is usua.lly denominated "brass;" but do you pretend th;1t this-. est[l,blishment was founded by Jesus Christ and !,is apostles? Do you pretend to holct your possessions immediately by n. grant from Goel; and thnt they are as much yours as my life and my limbs n.re mine? Why, yes, you are, at this time, very cnrious to relate, endeavouring to set up a something savouring of these pretensions, and are positively asserting' that you hold your possessions, and to the exclusion too of o.11 other Christian sects, by a right of prescr~Jtion; that is to so.y, o. right which existed before all written laws." After some very plain talk upon Harry the Eighth, and his deeply pious motives in setting up his Protestant-Popish church, he tells us:- " In the second year of the reign of Edward the Sixth, who was now only elei·en years old, who was at once supreme spiritual he11d of the church, and secular sovereign of the State, this Protestant church and religion were established. The Roman CathoEc religion having been abrogated, having been protested a!(ainst-, and declared to be idolatrons and damnable, a.II men were let loose to choose foi· themselves, each having the Bible in his hands, One sect had as much right to the churches and the tithes n.s n.nother sect; but this would never have done for the aristocracy. The remaining tithes, the oblations. the bishops' lands, the college lands-these were too valuable to be suffered to be scramble,l for, and though the 11ristocracy had protested against that church, to which they ha,1 belonged, and for the support of which they had been given, still they had no qun.rrel with the things themselves; they had not protested against the tithes, 11nd the !anus, and the oblations; they had only protested against their being in hands other thau their own .. The Catholic religion was idolatrous and damnable; but they saw nothing either idolatrous or damnable in the !antis, the tithes, antl the oblations. These, therefore, they reaolvecl to keep; but to keep them they must havo another church, and to tht1t church all must yield tithes nnd obbtions, howoverc~ntrary its creeus might be to the faith which the Scriptures taught them to adopt, or which they had been taught by their fathers from generation t.o gencmtion. '£he preamble of tho Act of Parliament, first ant! sl'coml Edward the Sixth, tells us tlrn.t tho king, in his great goodness, has appointee! the .cL'chbishop of Canterbury (Cranmer) and others to d1mv and make one meet, order, rite, a~,l fashion of common i.ud open pmyor and aclmiuistmtion of sacraments, to be h,1d ,rntl used in his Majesty's reo.lm o[ England n.ud Wales, tho wh eh at this time, by aid of the Holy Ghost, with ouo uniform agreement is of them coucluclecl, set forlh n.ud dcli,crctl to his highness (elei·en yeol's of age) to his great comfort and quietness of mind, mt1tule,l, 'The Book of Conwwn I'ra/Jel' and Administration of the Sacraments, and other Rite.; ""d Cel'emonies of the Church, aj)er the e,se of the Clmrch of Englaml' Wherefore, the Lonls spiritual and temporal in this present 1\,r!iamcnt assembled, considering as well the most godly tmva.il of the ldng"s highness (eleven years qj' "9') of tho Lord. Proteclor, ,in,\ of othor his highness's council, in g,1thcring nnd collecting the sn.itl archbishop and \came,\

nwn together, ""the godly prayers, rites, and ceremonioe in the Mid book mentioned; and the considol"lltions of e,ltering those thiuirs which he &ltered, and 1·etaining thoso things which he retained in the 11&i<1 book, b1;1t als_o th~ honour of God and great quietness, which, by the gr,ice of God, shall ensue,, do give hls lnghncss most hearty &ud lowly thanks for the11&me.' " Bearing in mind this assertion about the aid of tlw Holy Ghost, in this work, let us now come to the enact,nents. You, parsons, found the church's prescriptivo rights upon the I\Ssert\o~, tlwl tliere 11evei· was a11y Act of Pa,·liamentf01· tnki11g the beneficesawayfi•o,ntlie Catholics and givmg the111 t-0 I'rote..,tm1t..,; that the Catholic parish priests wero never ousted from their benl'fices bJ- Act of Parliament; tha,t they became converted in their sevcro.l parishes, or continued tc exercise their functions as before till the day of their death; or that they went a:way from their benefices w1thout force; so that, as they l1ad unquestionably o, prescriptive right to their benefices, the present parsons stand fairly in their shoes, and have a prescriptive rig/1/ too. Now, then, let us see how this matter st.'1.uds. The king had put forth a book of homilies and catechism. Priests had boon permitted to marry; and an act was soon after passed (2nd and 3rd Edward the Sixth, ch&pter 21) to allow priests to marry. Eyery inducement had been offered to withdraw the parish priests from their religion ; but still, with very few scandalous exceptions, they remained firm in their faith and their practice, at the time of the passing of this Act. The Act, therefore, provided that if any rector, vicar, perpetual curate, or other priest, with benefice, should in future say mass in the usual manner, and not use the Common Prayer Book, he should forfeit to the king one year·s revenue of his benefice, and be imprisoned for six mouths; that for a second offence he_ should be depri,ed of his benefice, and of all his spiritual promotions, and be impnsoned for one whole year; for a, third offence, imprisonment during his natural life; that if the priest had no benefice, he should be imprisoned for six months for the first ofl'.ence: and for the second offence should be imprisoned for his natural life! Thus did this gentle Chnstian church begin; thus did the angel of charity, humility, and humanity, preside at her birth. But the Act did not stop here, it went on to the laity; and it enacted that if any one should, by interludes, plays., songs., rhymes, or by other open words, declare or speak anything in derogation, depraving, or despising, the said Book of Common Prayer, penalty after penalty were to follow, till at last came the forfeiture of chattels to the king, a.ud imprison.meut during the natural life of the parLy ! ·• Here we have a faithful account of the BIRTH of this famous church, which simply put it to the priests and the people: •Here is this church; lake it; or, take pecuniary ruin and imprisonmentfor life;' and in the face of these undeniable facts, is there any one base enough to say' that the Catholic priests were not ousted by force and by Act of Parliament? '!.'be Act provides for the depriving of the party of his benefice, and of all spiritual promotion whatever, unless be apostatise from the Catholic religion; and it authorises patrons to appoint Protestant miuisters to succeed him, in just the same manner as if he were dead. ,vm Srn RoBJmT PEEL call this a 'a reformed Catholic church,' then? Will he again say, that the Protestant parsons stand in the prescriptive slwes of the Catholic priests? "But, the reader will say, did this Common Prayer Book always continue in use, after this .A.et was passed? Oh no! And now we have to see what sort of men those were who made this new church, a.ud to see well what their motives were. For very much depends upon this, when we are estin;iating the character of this church. "This church-ma.king king died at the end of about seven years, and was sncceeded on the throne by his sister Mary, who was a Catholic; and ~ho, proceeding: upo~ ~he settled coustitution and laws of the country, resolved upon restormg the Catholic relig10n. The Common PraYer-Book aristocracy, exceedingly alarmed at, this prospect; not so much :i.larmed. however, for the almost certain loss of the Common Prayer Bo,,k and the new church, as for the possible, and even probable loss of th"t immense mass of property of the church and the poor which they had got into their possession, by the means before mentioned, enkred into ~ negotiation with the queen, agreeing to give up their Common Prayer Boo/, and their Protestant religion; 11.grooing to bring back the Catholic religion into the country, and to punish parsons for_ not being Catholics, as they had punish~d them before for not Leiug Protestants; agreemg to coufess themselves to have bee':'- sch1~- matics; agr<xing tc receive absolutiou from the Pope for having rebe~led agamst his authority; agreeing to reinstate him in all his power in England, which they bef~re designated as abominable usw·patious; agreeing, above all things, to ab:ogate as schismatical that very Common Prayer Book which they had before declared m the preamblo t-0au Act of Parliament, f,o have been composed uy the 'aid of the Holy Ghost,' and which was, they ,;aid, made ' to the /w,wur of God;' agreeing to all ~his, if the queen_ would 0Ltai11 the consent of the Pope, and give her own consent, to suffer the"! to keep the wmwizse masses of prope>1y in land and in tithes, which, during the two precedrng rc1gus, they had !,'Tas1,ec1 /row the church and the poor! 'fhis is something so 1~0D:slrous, that 1 w~ul~ veutme to slate it upon no authonty short of that of an Act of I arhanu•Jlt; aud yet it 1s 1,y 1w weans tL<o worot tbat we have to behold on the part of these men who called them- ,elveo 110Uemcn and gei,//t11.,,~,, aud whose descendants coolly assume the same appellations!"

REVIEWS, 3i7 "But the second Act (1st Er,IZABETII1 chapter 2) brought back the Prayer B~ok again. The horrible men, whoso conduct we ho.ve been reviewing, had condemned their Prayer Book as Bchismcttical; had abolished it by their Acts; and had reinstated Catholic priests in the chmchos. They now, in tho Act of which I am speaking, ousted them again; reenctcted tho Oommon Prayer Book; and inflicted penitlties upon the priests who should refuse to apostatise by becoming Protestants and using this book in their churches. For the first offence, such priest was to forfeit a yc»r's revenue of his benefice, and ho imprisoned for six months. For a second offence he was to lose all his ecclesiastical prefonnents and possessions, and was, besides, to be imprisoned during the remainder of Ws life. If ho were a priest without a benefice, he was to be imprisoned, for the first offonco, during a whole year; for the second offence imprisoned during his whole life. For spealdng in derogation of the Prayer Book; or to ridicule the new religfon, by songs, plays, jests, of any sort, the offender was to forfeit a hundred marks for the first offence; four hundred marks for the second offence (equal to two thousand pounds of the money of this day); and for the third offence, to forfeit to the Queen all his goods and chattels, and bo imprisoned for life. Every person was compelled on Sundays and holydays, to attend at the church, to hear this common pmyer, under various pecunfary penalties, and in failure of paying the penalties, to be imprisoned. Bishops, •Archdeacons, and other ordiuaries, were to have power for inflicting these punishments. This Act of confiscation, of ruin, of stripes, of death, was enforced with all the rigour that imagination can conceive. The Queen reigned for forty-Jive years, and these forty-fiTe years were spent in deeds of such cruelty as the world had never heard of or read of before; and all for the purpose of compelling her people to submit to this established church." The following sentences we place in capitals, and call the earnest attention of thoughtful men to their assured truth and solemn importance :- " THE MAIN THING, HOWEVER, TO IlE KEPT IN VIEW HERE, IS THE FACT, WHICH ALL THESE ACTS OF PARLIAll[ENT SO FULLY CONFIRM, THAT TlIIS CHURCH WAS CREATED BY ACTS OF PARLIAllIE.'iT: THAT IT HAS NO EXISTENCE AS A CHURCH, THAT rr HAS NO RITE, NO CEREI\IONY1 NO CREED, NO ARTICLE OF F..1.ITH, WHICll FI.AS ~OT SPR~G OUT OF AN ACT OF THE p ARLIAMENT; AND THAT THERE IS :SOTHING OF PRESCRIPTIO~ BELONGING TO IT, FROM ITS FIRST BEING NAMED AMONGST ME..'<, O'.'ITIL THE PRESE..'IT HOUR."

"How came there to be people called Dissenters ?" is responded to in letter II. and then in letter III. the question is discussed, " What is the foundation of the domination of the church over the Dissenters 1" Many of the remarks upon this head have now happily lost their force by reason of relief granted by our legislature ; but the greatest of all grievances still remains, and is well put in true Cobbett style:- " All these exclusions, however, great as the injuriousness of them is, unjust as they are towards the great body of the people, and degrading a.s they are in their tendency, are, all put together, a mere trifle, compared with tile compulsion upon the Dissenters to give the fruits of their estates and the fruits of their earnings, for the purpose of supporting the establisllecl clergy and church. Is there anything that can be conceivecl more hostile to natural justice, than for men to be compelled to take away from the means of supporting their families a considerable part of the fruit of their labour, and to give it to men for preaching a doctrine ill which they do not believe, and for performing a service in which their consciences forbid t_hem to join? If there be anything more hostile to natural justice than this, I should like to hrtvc it pointed out to me. To be sure they are no longer compelled, on pain of banishment, or de"th, to go into the churches and call Goel to witness th"t they reverence that which they abhor; but they are compelled to give thei,. 1no11ey or their goods in support of it; and this indeed was all that tb.e banishment "nd the hanging were intended to insure. If tho church-makers of Edward ancl Elizabeth could have obtained secu,·ity for getting money of the Dissenters, as quietly as it is now got, they would never have had any Acts of Pttrlittment to compel them to go to church ; they would have been as' liberal' as our present P"rsous now are; tho flocks might have roamed where they hacl liked, as they do now: the shepherds having taken care to secure the .fleece." Allowing for the fact that this trenchant tre,itise appeared more thanthlrly years ago, and is therefore in many of its expre8sions, a little out of date, we still think it very seasotmble, and believe th,tt a liberal distribution of it would do much to aid the progress of public sentiment towards perfect and universal religious equality. The Anglican State Establishment is a standing insult. to Dissenters, its forced support is downright oppression, its ,tscendancy is ghmng injustice, its very existence is a crime. A REVIEW BY C. H. SPURGEON. NDER the title of "The Seven Curses of London,"* Mr. Greenwood, the "Amateur Casual," has produced a sadly

OO~-- 0 interesting book-a book whose every page woulJ lie bedewed with tears, if all readers were like in heart to Him who wept over Jerusalem. The curses so vividly set before us in this volume are not such as are so ea! led by idle impatience, because they flutter the deeorum of gentility, 0r disturb the quiet of heartlessness; they are real curses, deep and deadly, withering, soul-destroying, damnable: the descriptions given are all the more weighty, because they are not written from the point of view of the professional philanthropist or the spiritual teacher; if the merel_vliterary man sees so much to lament in our leviathan city, what may still clearer eyes discern! Alter reading Mr. Greenwood's record, we are conscious of intense pain and anguish, mingled witl1 vehement resolve to leave no means untried to alleviate the wretchedness of this Babylon. We wish every Christian man could be made aware of the vict:, the destitution, and the mise1·y whiuh surround him; it would make him a better servant of the Lord. We are a vast deal too comfortable. We simper with complacency at the good which we are doing, when. like Mrs. Partington•~ mop, we are srarcely pushing back one wave of the seething ocean of iniquity around us. At om· pious gatherings we half persuade ourselves that the world is being conv,erted. and that gross vice is a rara av-is in the land, and all the while· the devil, with almost uudisputed sway, rules the masse~, and devours them at hi~ will. Those lines of first-class residences, those lung terraces of respectable houses, those miles of pretty villas, those leagues of bu~y shops-one • "Tb.e Seven Curoes of Lon.Ion,'' by J amos Greon woocl, the .\.lllateur CasuaL Loudon, Slnnley Rivers and Co.

rides along thrnl by the hour, and feels that London is great, flomishinl!', wealthy, orderly; a\', but turn out of that broad thoroughfare, stop at Paradise Collrt or Ro~emary Alley, take your walks a\Jroa<l where many poor you see, note the ragg-e<l children, the filthy Irishwomen, the harlots, the drunkards, the swarms of villanous-lookiug big bo,rs; an<l uow, as you return, siek from the reek of gin and the mustineRs of rags, you learn that London is poor, wretched, lawless, horrible. It is ll"ell to ham the rose-water removed, and the rose-colour washed off awhile. Another excuse for niggardly giving and shorthanded workingwill be torn away, when we are no longer in ignorance of our city's Ii w ful needs. The first of the sefen cur~es mentioned by our author is "neglected children." Well may the writer call it a startling fact, that in E11gla11d and Wales, three hunllred and fifty thousand children, under the age of s1xt.een, are dependent more or less on parish authorities for maintenauee; in London alone, one lmndred thousand children wander in de~titution, preparing for our gaols or for early graves. Children of r 1,e gutter, their f11od is scant, their lodging foul, their elothing rag!!erl. Eren when blessPd with a mother, the young Arabs neither fare rnmptuously by night nor by day. Cradled in a gooseberry sieve, or 11esLled in an egg box, the babies of the poorest class h<lve no injurious luxury to enenate them. St.range facts come under our author's own observation. "Accompanied by a friend, he was on a visit of exploration into the little-known regions of Baldwin's GardenF, in Leather Lane, and entering a cellar there, the family who oceupied it were discovered in a state of dreadful commotion. The mother, a tall, bony, ragged shre1~, had a baby tucked under one arm, while she was using the other by the aid of a pair of dilapidated nozzleless bellows in inflicting a tremenrlous beating on a howling young- gentleman of about. eleven years old. 'Tut! tut! what is the matter, Mrs. Donelly? Rest your arm a rnoment, now, and tell us all about it.' 'Matther ! shure it's matther enough to dhrive a poor widdy beyaut her senses!' And then her rage turning to sorrow, she in -pathetic terms dE.scribed how that she left tliat bad hoy Johnny only for a few moments in charge of the 'darlint comfortable ashleap in her bashket,' and that he had neglecled his duty, and that the IJaste of a donkey had smelt her out, and 'ate her elaue out o' berl.' . . . It was not long after the ineident of the goosehPrry sie1·e, that I discovered in one small room in whieh a family of six resided, three little children, varyiug in age from three to eight, perhaps, ~tark naked. It was 00011 of a summer's day, and there tl~ey were nude as fore8t monkeys, and so hideously dirty th~t every r!bbo11e in their poor wasted little bodies showed plain, and 111 colour hke rnahogany. Soon as I put my head in at the door they scattered, 1;ca1ed as rabLits, to the 'IJed,' an arrangement of evil-smell mg floek ;,ud olcl polato-bach, and I was informed by the mother that they had 11nt a rn,,, t•> wear au<l had been iu tlieir present condition for morn than three m:i1t1,s." if iliese things be true of children left under the care of poor pe1111iless widows, wliat a plea we have fo1· our orpha11a!!P, and how gn.11 c,f'ul ~110ul<l we a11d our band of helpers be that we are allowed L(I du a little to prevent weh mi~erv.

and endowed with virtues s11ch as wholesome food possesses. Did the reader ever see the young market hunters at sueh a 'feed,' sa_v in the month of Aagust or September? It is a spectacle to be witnessed only by early risers who can get as far as Covent Garden by the time that the wholesale dealing in the open falls slack-whieh will be about eight o'clock; and it is not to be believed unless it is seen. They wil I gather about a muck heap and gobble up plums, a sweltering mass of decay, and oranges and apples that have quite lost their original shape and colour, with the avidity of duel{s or pigs. I speak acc:ording to my knowledge, for I have seen them at it. I have seen one of these gaunt wolfish little children with his tattered cap full of plums of a oort one of whieh I would not have permitted a child of mine to eat for all the money in the Mint, and this at a season when the sanitary authorities in their desperate alarm at the spread of cholera had turned bill sticker~, and were begging and imploring the people to abstain from, this, that, and the other, and especially to beware of fruit unless perfectly sound and ripe. Judging from the earnestness with which this last provision was urged, there must have been cholera enough to have slain a dozen strong men in that little ragamuffin's cap, and yet he munehed on till that frowsy receptacle was emptied, finally licking his fingers with ,i relish. It was not for me to forcibly dispossess the boy of a p1,ize that made him the envy of his plumless companions, but L ~poke to the market beadle about it, asking him if it would not be possible, knowing the propensities of these poor little wretches, so to dispose of the poisonous offal that they could not get at it; but he replied tha.t it was nothing to do with him what they ate so loug as they kept their hands from picking and stealing; furthermore, he politely intimated, that 'unless I had nothing better to do,' there was no call for me to trouble myself about the 'little warmint.,' whom nothing would hurt. He confided to me his private belief that they were' made inside something alter the orsestretch, and that farriers' nails would'nt come amiss lo 'ern if they could only get 'em down.'" Very painful are the results of enquiries into the parentage of these '' rank outsiders" of humanity, these wretched waifs and strays of the race ; and if possible, even worse are the revelations concerning the baby-farming, and other forms by which certain of these poor little souls are reared, or rather, murdered wholesale. Advertistmenls for nurse children, and for babes to be adopted, mean a great deal more than unsuspecting readers have usually imagined. How many babes have passed into t>ternity throu!!h the "ha'p'orth of bread and a ha'p'ortl1 ol' milk a-day" system, eternity alone can reveal. No longer need we wonder at the large proportion of infantile mortality. But what unuatural, brutal sin does all this mean ! Their object is RO praiseworthy, and the need of every wellintentioned effort so manifest, that it is a pity to throw cold water on any earnest tempPrance movement. If teetotalers are rather too prone to treat contemptuously the efforts of those who do not adopt their modes of operation, there is I he more reason whv the true tem'.)erance but non-teetotal mrn should behave with courtesy to his more irritable fellow worker, for whom he is bound to entertain a kindly esteem. This demon of drink must be fonght, for it swallows men bv thousands, makes their homes wretched, their chiiflren paupers: and their souls the prey of the devil. There should be combined and vigorous action among ail temperate men for rnch a control of licenses that the dens of drunkenness shonld be made far le8s numerous, to say the least, and if we went in for still severer restrictions so much the better. We are unmistakably overdone with gin-palaces and beer-houses ; they are thrust upon us at every street-corner; they are multiplied beyond all pretence of demand. Not the public goori but the publican's good appears to be the aim of the licensers. Quiet neighbourhoods cannot spring up because the beer-house rises simnltaneously; or if such a thing should for a few months be seen under heaven as a sober region, universally respectable, and guiltless of int.oxication, the Bacchanalian missionary soon opens his temple and conve1-ts the population to the common error of drinking way~. It is true, the demand for drink creates the supply, bnt it is as surely true that the all-surrounding omnipresence of the stimulant suggests, and propagates the craving. At any rate, no two opinions can exist upon one point, namely, that the accursed habit of intoxication lies at the root of the main part of London's poverty, misery, and crime. Betting gamblers, in the sixth place, come in for their share of our author's condemnation. "There can be no doubt that the vice of gambling is on the increase among~t the English working-classe~. Of this no better proof is afforded than in the modern multiplication of those newspapers specially devoted to matters 'sportive.' T1venty years ago there were but three or four sporting newspapers published in London; now there are more than a dozen." Those who occupy the highest mnks of the sncial scale have the fearful responsibility of rendering gambling fashionable, and their example has had its influence upon all ranks, until even children beL their shillings and the lads of the gutter cry the odds. A tribe of '' prophets," blacklegs, and advertisers, feed npon this growing vice, s11·arming about it like flies around carrion. Marvellous are the fortune~ to be made by "putting on" a few pounds, and rich are the promised gains of even a dozen postage stamp~, staked upon the horse whose name will be communicated upon the receipt ot' a fee; more marvellous still is the senseless folly which can be duped by such manifest quackery. - "Of all manner of advertising betting gamblers, however, none are so pernicions, or work such lamentnble evil against society, as those who, with devilish cunnirrg,appeal to the young and inexperienced-the factory lad and youth of the counting house or the shop. Does anyone <loubt if horse-racing has attractions for those whose tender age renders it complimentary to style them' young men'? Let him on tl1c day of any

~nown that the proprietors of the Sunday Ti'mes, Belrs Life, and other JOUrnnls of a sporting tendency, in their zeal to outdo each other in presenting the earliest possible information to the public, are at the tronble and expense of securing the earliest possible telegram of the resn lt of a horse-race, aud exhibiting it enlarged on a broad-sheet in their ~hop-windows. Let us take the Sunday Times, for instance. The office of this most respectable of sporting newspapers is situated near the corner of Fleet-street at Ludgate-hill; and wonderful is the spectacle there to be seen on the afternoon of the great equine con.test on Ep~om downs. On a small scale, and making allowance for the absence of the living provocatives of excitement the scene is a reproduction of what at that moment, or shortly since, has taken place on the race-course itself. Three o'clock is about the time the great race is run at Epsom, and at that time . the Fleet-street crowd begins to gather. It streams in from the north, from the east, from the south. At a glance it is evident that the members of it are not idly curious merel.v. It is not composed of ordinary pedestrians who happen to be coming that way. Butcher-lads, from the neighbouring great meat-market, come bareheaded and perspiring down Ludgate-hill, and at a pace that tells how exclusively their eager minds are set on racing: all in blue working-smocks, and with the grease and blood of their trade adhering to their naked arms, and to their hobnailed boots, and to their hair. Hot and palpitating they reach the obelisk in the middle of the road, and there they take their stand, with their e_yes steadfastly fixed on that at present blank and innocent window that shall presently tell them of their fate. "I mention the butcher-boys first, because, for some unknown reason, they undoubtedl_v are foremost in the rank of juvenile bettors. In the days when the .Fleet-lane betting abomiuation as yet held out against the police authorities, and day after day a narrow alley beliind the squalid houses there served as sLanding room for as many 'professional' betting men, with their boards and money-pouches, as could crowd in a row, an observer standing at one end of the lane might count three blue frocks for one garment of any other colour. But though butcher-bovs show conspicuously among the anxious Fleet-street rush on a Derby-day, they are not in a majority by a long way. To bet on th€ 'Derbv' is a mania that afflicts all trades; and streaming up Farringdon-~treet may be seen repre~entatives of almost every craft that practises within the City's limits. There is the inky printer's boy, hot from the' :nachine-room,' with his grimy face and his cap made of a ream wrapper; there is the jeweller's apprentice, with his bibbed white apron, ruddy with the powder of rouge and borax; and the paperstainer's lad, with the variegated splashes of the pattern of his last 'length' yet wet on his ragged breeches; and a hundred others, all hurrying pell-mell to the one spot, and, in nine cases out of t.en, wiLh the guilt of having 'slipped out' visible on their streaming faces. Take tl1eir ages as they cungregate in a crowd of five h11ndred and more (tLey are expected in such numbers that special policemen are provided

While the betting-men were making a stand in Farringdon-street in the open air against the city authonties, Mr. Greenwood made the acquaintance of the subject of 111,i story. " He was not remarkable amongst the betting blackguards he mingled with on account of the active share he took in the questionable husine~s in which they were engaged; on the contrary, he seemed quite out of place with them, and though occasionally one would patronise him with a nod, it was evident that he was' nothing to them,' either as a comrade or a gull to be plucked. He appeared to be drawn towards them by a fascination he could not resist, but which he deplored and wlls ashamed or. It was customary in those times for the prn~pnous horse-betting gambler to affect the genteel person who could afford to keep a' man,' aud to press into his service some poor ragged wretch glad to earn a sixpence by wearing his mastn's 'card of terms' round his neck for the inspection of any perrnn inclined to do bu~iness. The tall shabby young fellow's chief occupation consisted in wandering restlessly from one of these betting-card bearers to another, evidently with a view to comparing 'prices' and 'odds' offered on this or that horse; but he never bet. I don't believe that his pecuniary affairs would have permitted him, even though a bet as low as twopence-ha! f'penny might be laid. "I ,ms always on the look-out for my mi~erable-looking young friend whenever I passed that way, and seldom failed to find him. He seemed to possess for me a fascination something like that which horse-betting possessed for him. One afternoon, observing him alone and looking even more miserable than I had yet seen him, as he slouched along the miry pavement towards Holborn, I fouud means to start a conversation witll him. My object was to learn who and what he "·as, and ,Yhrther he was really as miserable as he looked, and whether there WHS any help !or him. BY J. A. SPURGEON, "\TES, Mr. Editor, Smoke! You say that "it is not suited to your .I_ columns, which never contain such matter." Very true. "Your readers don't like smoke." Kor do we; and yet how much of it both you and your readers must put up with in this world 1 You cannot ]Jass an act of parliament for the universe, and write ~p, a~ they do in Continental railway carriages, "No smoking allowed m this compartment." There is a certain amount of nuisance which we must shut our el'es to, and bear as best we may. Not that we wish you to shut your eyes to our paper, but rather that your readers ma}'. consider thal. there is no use in uying to banish out of existence all thrngs tlmt offend, nor

SMOKE.

of losing our temper if we cannot snerPed in making everyone sr1uare into our views upon all qnesti0ns. Yet we know, for instance, some ministers who cannot, make use of a deacon's warm heart and earnest fire of spirit, hecanse he h,1s Hmoke with it, which makes other people's eyes s11iart at time~. we arlmit, hat which seems to he a part of his beinl!-at least, it is so for the present. Now, what foll_v to begin h.v complaints, nnd trying to correct the wrong without utilising the g-ood ! but some people must commenee wit.h a g-eneral scold all round, to set matters right hefore they Rtart. What imperfect instrnments we are at best; and yet., though we mnst he offensive to God's holiness, he is pleaser! to work with us and through us. This should make us tolera11t of others' weakne~ses. We remember a deacon of considerable i11flnence and talent, just joined to an ill-regulated country church, creating much mischief by trying to put out the smoke at once: the good people trembled for the few sparks of fire, and rose for the defence of the feeble flame, and in the end it was nearly quenched hy their un- ~eemly disputes. Now it would have heen far better to have fanned the sparks into a flame, and thus have done away with the smoke. To overcome evil with good is the scriptural plan. We were wet through, the other day, in a country walk, and stepped into a lone house to dry ourselves by a turf fire, which was eertainly very primitive, and we dare say very wasteful of fuel, nnd certainly smoked foriously at times; but we rejoiced in its flame. Now, some modern reformers would have commenced bv raking out the fire in order to insert a re!!'istered sto,e of latest fashion, which would burn the best of coal_ with admirable economy, but not the turf from the common, which would there flare out in a few minutes. No, we must let some things alone, and put them away bv indirect means, or else, in preventing smoke, we may exhaust the fire. Our Lord permits the tare~ to grow, rather than run the risk of pulling up wheat. It is no argmnent, either for tares or smoke, that we leave them; they are evils. hut to remove ttem might mean the creating of yet greater ones, and therefore, for the present, we let them remain. You think we mean to advocate smoking? No, indeed. we onlv mean to imply that some amount of smoke aprears in this world to l{e inevitable, and we want to have it rightly dealt with. Our coals will smoke when bnrning, therefore, we have a chimney, and the point is to make r.he smoke !!'O up that chimney. Have yon succeeded? We ha_-e· not. Whv do chimners smoke? we mean smoke the wrong wav. It is 0

rather a rjJeasant sight to see the smoke of one's chimney far off when returning home, hut oh ! to see the other end of that chimney smoking, when you are at home, that is not so pleasant. You know the effeec upon your line11 of those puff~ on a brisk Mareh day, especially if there be anv fine muslin about. You have seen the shower of blacks which condurleR the scene, and the residne of smuts upon all your ehoice treasures in the room. We are sure our readers will understand all this. as ,,·ho ]ms not witnessed it? Well then, do your best to send all smoke up the chimney. Of course, the right thing is to consume your own smoke in a chimney tall enough for the purpose, but if that mav not be, then send it up the short chimney out of every one's wa_v. And, moreover, help to send other people's smoke np them too. Some persons

execrate snch people, we <'an find no words too strong. Take a case we hn,e seen at times. The minister is not so popular ns he was, his sPrmons are not so full of life, and his ministrations are not so acceptable. Pcrhr.ps he is in trouble, and needs heln, or he may be me·ntally and plwsicall:r weary, and requires a rest. There is not so much fire and ~ little m~re si:noke in his disco~irses. What is to be done? Pray for him. and aid him through the difficulty 1s the proper thing. Give l1im more fuel for the fire, heap some coals upon him and blow cheery worrls of comfort into him. But this would not suit these individuals :::o they pour cold water on him, and go and whisper here and there' " That all is not quite as it need to be, the_v and many others are dis~ ,;atisfierl." And when they have damaged his energ_v by sufficient coldness and indifference, they arrange to go and poke him up with a dozen sharp insinuations as to what can he the matter? Does he mean to seek another sphere? Does h~ think the cause needs a chang-e of ministr_v? And thus they soon contrive to make more smoke, till all the fire seems to die out, and miniRter and people become cold and dead. We have seen advertised a" Patent Fire Extinguisher;" and we have 1,nown some church members that we would gladly have given away for that purpose. Now all this is as smoke in our nostrils. We would as Fonn that a man asked us to sit in his house with a smoky chimney, as listen to his slander and faultfiuding about his neighbours, and eRpeciall_v about his minister and fellow Christians. Charity thinketh no ill, and we are sure that it speaketh none. Let your fire of love have ncme of this black sediment and smoke of mischief about it. We can tolerate smoke if there be any heat, but without some fire we are at a loss to discover its use. Smoke is a nuisance, whether in a room, a church, or a railway carriage; and we know some other things that we abominate as smoke besides what comes from the fire-place. Did ,on ever listen to the conversation in an ordinary evening· partyeven· the better sort, composed of persons who make some profession of love for hig-her and holier things? We confess t.hat we have been sickened with the twiddle-twaddle that is sure to make up the staple of the int.errourse. All iR smoke, and of no use to body, mind, or soul. 0 that Christians would remember that for every idle word that we speak we must giYe an account in the <lay of judgment ! How much of mere verbiag-e is to Le found in many of our devotional 1:xercises ! h that not merely smoke which does not come from the heart and is not inRtinct with 'the fire of true desire? Better bring a few ;nrds all in a ft,une of earnest importunate pleading, than merely ,monlrler ou for half an hour in commonplace repetition of sentences whieh have no life in them. What a Rmoke must come up at times frnm the altar of our chapels in the place of the flame, bright and 1111-coM~nming-, which oug-ht ever to be there! May God by his Spirit intensify our half-heartedness into true worship at all times.

may inst1mce the incense, the millinery, and the bobbino-s about of a high-church ritual, and, for the matter of that, many thin<rs in the ordinary church service also. Who regards the duty of sp7msors at lrnptism as anything else than a mere bank of smoke, unsubstantial and useless? As to coufirmation, it is as dense a cloud of Rmoke a~ 4:Ver the church of Rome devised for the blinding of souls. What good can the hands of mortal man confer upon the heads and hearts of youth, who have no faith in Christ, and if they are believers, what do they want with any other priest than the One who has rerfeeted for ever them that are sanctified? We were just now reading the church of England's ordination service, and we thought we never saw more smoke from the bottomless pit than is manifest in some parts of it. We agree with the Bishop of Oxford, that the phraseology " is the most blasphemous frivolity, if it be not the deepest truth," and we arid that it certainly is not the latter. We quote the words used by the Bishop, while his hands are upon the head of the would-be priest: "Receive the Holy Ghost for the office and work of a priest in the church of God now committed unto thee by the imposition of our hands. Wiiose sins thou dost forgive they are forgiven, and whose sins thou dost retain they are retained. And be thou a faithful dispenser of the word of God and of his holy sacraments; in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen." Now, if that is not smoke of sulphur aud brimstone, we know not what is. Mortal man to confer upon his foll.ow mortal the power of forgiving sin, in the name of Lhe Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost! Now we turn to some words of the Rev. Henry Melville, to show that even evangelical preachers attach such a value to this ordination, that the offiee is exalted above common sense, to say nothing about Scripture :-'· The ordained preacher is a messenger-a messenger from the God of the whole earth. His mental capacity may be weali:-that is nothing. His speech may he contemptible-that is nothing. His knowledge may be circumscribed-we say not that is nothing, but "IIC say that whatever the man's qualifications, he should rest in his office. . . . " Now, is not all that smoke which blinds and deludes, and which we must abominate as of the ver_y essence of popery? What we want is the God-given fire of the Spirit, and without tltat we care for no otlice, real or assumed. Away with it as a nuisance and a superstition noo to be tolerated in this enlightened age. One use of sm11ke is not to Lie overlooked. We have, near our Tabernacle, au erection made by a wealthy intlividual, whose amusement it is to attend all Lhe fires about; a 1d in this outlook a man is stationed to watch for smoke which indicates a house on tire. Those who live near a coal mine know too well what a dense cloud of smoke rising up the shaft and mouth of the pit unhappily indicates. Help is required, and men are in distress; perhaps death is plying its awful trade below. T!iere is never any want or interest about a tire iu London. A crowd is sure to gather in a few minute~, and where all the ~mall bo_l's Rpring from at once we have 11ever yet been able to discover. Everyone is arrested and aroused when a house is on fire. Would tha~ the deadly pall of sin, which rises from e\'cry street, and bangs darkly

!lo"· often we may ci~t,ect such sign~ of iniquity in our own heat·ts, or Ill our churches! We must not wait t.ill the mis0hief ha.s gained head, and bnr,t out into an open flame. ,v e must at once use all means to crnsh OL1t the source of ill before it breaks forth in~o an irresistible floo~. We fauc_v thflt some of onr readers may have expected an ~pinion unon the fashion of tobacco smoking-, which is gr~wing upon w1 as a mtion. Well, we do not smc1ke; we think it a most admi rahle way of raisin!! mone_v for the public exchequer, and we therefore feel a debt of gratitu,1.e t.o t,hose patriotic individuals wbo contribute so much to our national fund ; but as to anythin\\' further, we have nothin~ to say.
